paragraphs: Sequential decision makers often have to choose their next action before feedback from earlier actions arrives. This paper studies stochastic delays across several settings: bandits, single-agent Markov decision processes, and multi-agent Markov games. Its central question is how to preserve efficient learning when feedback arrives late, across this broad family of problems.

The proposed framework converts an algorithm designed for instantaneous feedback into one that handles stochastic delays. The starting algorithm must have a multi-batched structure, so the conversion applies to that class of algorithms rather than to arbitrary learning procedures. This reduction makes existing algorithms reusable: different compatible starting methods produce delayed-feedback methods for different decision-making settings.

The authors show that these combinations match or improve earlier results for bandits and tabular single-agent and multi-agent problems. They also extend the investigation to function approximation, where learning uses a parameterized representation rather than an explicit table. The contribution is a common theoretical route to sample-efficient learning with delays, connecting results that would otherwise require separate algorithm designs.
neurips-2023-a-reduction-based-framework.tldr: A reduction converts compatible multi-batched decision-making algorithms into sample-efficient methods for stochastic delayed feedback.

paragraphs: Learning from a demonstration becomes harder when the learner sees what happened but not which actions produced it. AIME addresses this observation-only imitation problem using a world model learned from the agent's own previous experience. The model provides a basis for connecting observed behavior to actions the agent could take with its own body.

Training has two phases. First, the agent learns its world model by maximizing an evidence lower bound, an objective used to fit probabilistic models. Next, it receives expert observations for a new task and treats its policy as an inference model. The policy is learned by making the demonstration more probable under the combined policy and world model.

Here, zero-shot has a specific meaning: after receiving the demonstration, the agent needs neither further world-model training nor online environment interactions. It still uses previously collected experience and performs policy inference from the demonstration. Experiments on Walker and Cheetah in the DeepMind Control Suite report better imitation performance than the state-of-the-art baselines evaluated.
neurips-2023-action-inference-by-maximis.tldr: AIME uses a previously learned world model to infer imitation policies from observation-only demonstrations without new environment interactions.

paragraphs: A controller may need to manage a continuously changing system while paying a cost each time it observes that system. This makes observation timing part of the decision problem. The paper formalizes continuous-time control with costly observations, motivated by settings such as medicine, low-power systems, and resource management.

Its theoretical result shows that regularly spaced observations are suboptimal in certain environments: irregular timing can yield higher expected utility. This is a conditional result, not a claim that irregular schedules always win. It establishes that fixing a regular observation schedule can exclude better solutions, making the timing of information collection worth optimizing alongside control.

The authors construct an initial method using an offline continuous-time model within a model predictive control planner. A heuristic threshold on the variance of simulated reward rollouts guides observations. Experiments in several continuous-time environments, including a cancer simulation, support the theoretical findings. The optimal method remains an open problem; the demonstrated contribution is the formulation, timing result, and an initial practical approach.
neurips-2023-active-observing-in-continu.tldr: The paper shows that irregular observation timing can improve continuous-time control with observation costs and tests an initial heuristic planner.

paragraphs: Cooperative reinforcement learning must connect individual agents' choices to the success of the whole team. Learning that relationship directly can be complex. GoMARL introduces an intermediate level: dynamically formed groups of agents whose contributions help explain the value of the team's joint actions.

The method expresses joint action-values through a combination of group-level values. An automatic grouping mechanism produces both the groups and their action-values without requiring domain knowledge to define the groups beforehand. These smaller units provide more detailed guidance for policy improvement while still contributing to the team objective. Grouping therefore becomes part of the learning process rather than a fixed organizational choice.

A hierarchical policy-learning mechanism encourages agents within a group to develop similar policies while different groups maintain diverse strategies. Experiments on StarCraft II micromanagement and Google Research Football support the method's effectiveness. Component studies further examine how grouping contributes to performance. Together, the findings support learned subgroups as a useful structure for improving cooperation and learning efficiency in the evaluated team tasks.
neurips-2023-automatic-grouping-for-effi.tldr: GoMARL learns dynamic agent groups and group-level values to make cooperative reinforcement learning more efficient.

paragraphs: Neural networks can predict visual brain responses accurately, but those predictions can be difficult to interpret. This paper trains networks from scratch to predict brain responses to natural images, then examines which image features drive their units. The aim is to use a predictive model to investigate spatial preferences across visual brain regions.

The authors adapt network dissection into a method called brain dissection. It explores properties beyond object categories, including depth, surface orientation, curvature, and relationships between objects. This provides a way to investigate how modeled responses relate to the geometry and arrangement of a scene, rather than only the identities of its contents.

The analysis finds that ventro-lateral regions favor closer, curvier features, while medial and parietal regions favor more varied, flatter three-dimensional elements. Parietal regions show a distinctive preference for spatial relations. Scene-selective regions also differ: the retrosplenial complex favors distant and outdoor features, while occipital and parahippocampal place areas favor proximity and verticality, with the former also favoring indoor elements. These results demonstrate the potential of interpretable predictive models to reveal finer spatial selectivity.
neurips-2023-brain-dissection-fmri-train.tldr: Brain dissection interprets networks trained on brain responses to reveal differing spatial-feature preferences across visual cortical regions.

paragraphs: Recognizing objects and attributes separately does not establish that a model knows which attribute belongs to which object. Cola tests this distinction through text-to-image retrieval. A model must select an image with the requested arrangement while rejecting distractors containing the same objects and attributes in a different configuration.

The benchmark contains about 1,200 composed queries covering 168 objects and 197 attributes across roughly 30,000 images. The authors also compare six ways of adapting two pretrained vision-language models. Among the evaluated approaches, the best strategy trains a multimodal attention layer over frozen image and language features, allowing those features to be considered jointly.

Training such layers on CLIP performs better than tuning a larger FLAVA model that already contains pretrained multimodal layers. Both models reach comparable levels with the proposed adaptation, suggesting that training with contrastive attribute-object data matters substantially. Simpler tuning succeeds on CREPE but falls short on Cola, and the best adaptation still trails human accuracy. The findings identify both a useful adaptation strategy and a remaining compositional reasoning gap.
neurips-2023-cola-a-benchmark-for-compos.tldr: Cola tests whether image retrieval models bind attributes to the correct objects and exposes a persistent gap despite effective multimodal adaptation.

paragraphs: Vision Transformers have been observed to respond relatively weakly to changes in input-token order. DropPos addresses this by making spatial location the target of a self-supervised training task. Instead of supplying all position information, it asks the model to recover missing locations from what image patches look like.

The method removes a large random subset of positional embeddings and trains the model to classify patch positions among the possible locations. It also keeps only some patches visible, increasing the difficulty and discouraging trivial solutions. Because visually similar patches may plausibly occupy different locations, position smoothing and attentive reconstruction relax the demand for exact position recovery in such cases.

Across downstream benchmarks, DropPos outperforms supervised pretraining and is competitive with state-of-the-art self-supervised alternatives. The findings suggest that explicitly practicing spatial reasoning improves location awareness in Vision Transformers. The approach matters because its training signal comes from the spatial organization of the image itself, while acknowledging that visual appearance does not always uniquely identify a patch's position.
neurips-2023-droppos-pre-training-vision.tldr: DropPos pretrains Vision Transformers to recover missing patch positions, encouraging spatial awareness while accommodating visually ambiguous patches.

paragraphs: An agent may have to act even when its latest state observation is delayed or missing. This paper studies the learning difficulty created by those conditions in reinforcement learning. The issue concerns access to the current state itself: the agent must make decisions with an incomplete or outdated view of the system.

The authors establish near-optimal regret bounds for both delayed and missing observations. Regret measures the performance shortfall accumulated while learning. Their bounds have square-root dependence on the product of the original system's state count, action count, and number of episodes, together with a polynomial dependence on the horizon and suppressed logarithmic factors. The state-action dependence is optimal despite the more difficult policy and planning problems.

The paper also characterizes the best policy achievable under impaired observability relative to the optimal value with full observations. This separates two questions: how efficiently an agent can learn with its available information, and how much that information restriction affects achievable performance. The results support efficient learning in the studied settings without claiming that delayed or missing observations leave optimal performance unchanged.
neurips-2023-efficient-rl-with-impaired-.tldr: The paper establishes near-optimal learning guarantees for reinforcement learning with delayed or missing state observations.

paragraphs: A long video does not necessarily require long-term understanding: a question about it might be answerable from a brief moment. EgoSchema is designed to evaluate the temporal understanding actually demanded by video questions. It contains more than 5,000 human-curated multiple-choice question-answer pairs derived from Ego4D, spanning over 250 hours of natural human activity.

Each question offers five answers and refers to a three-minute clip. The authors introduce temporal certificate sets to characterize a task's intrinsic temporal understanding length, going beyond clip duration alone. Under this measure, EgoSchema's temporal lengths exceed those of the next closest dataset by more than 5.7 times, indicating that its questions demand information across substantially longer stretches.

The evaluated video-language models struggle with this benchmark. Even models with billions of parameters score below 33% accuracy, compared with 20% for random guessing and about 76% for humans. These results reveal a substantial gap on the tested questions and position EgoSchema as a diagnostic resource for developing systems that understand extended activity rather than isolated moments.
neurips-2023-egoschema-a-diagnostic-benc.tldr: EgoSchema measures genuinely extended video understanding and reveals a large performance gap between evaluated models and humans.

paragraphs: Some causal effects can be learned by combining observational data with experimental data. Generalized identification asks whether the available distributions together determine a target causal effect. Although this identification problem has a theoretical solution, turning its answers into reliable estimates from finite samples remains challenging.

This paper develops a general estimator for effects that satisfy generalized identification. Its key step is to express any such effect using generalized multi-outcome sequential back-door adjustments. This representation makes the identification expression amenable to estimation, linking the theoretical statement that an effect is recoverable to a procedure for estimating it from data.

The resulting estimator has multiple robustness properties against bias, and the authors analyze its convergence as sample sizes grow. Experimental illustrations and simulations support the theory. The scope remains g-identifiable effects: the method estimates effects that the available observational and interventional information can identify. Its contribution is a broadly applicable estimation route within that scope, with robustness properties that address the practical gap between an identification formula and an estimate based on limited observations.
neurips-2023-estimating-causal-effects-i.tldr: A general, multiply robust estimator turns causal effects identifiable from combined observational and experimental distributions into estimable quantities.

paragraphs: Predicting quantum chemical properties benefits from knowing a system's three-dimensional geometry. However, obtaining the accurate geometries used by many prediction models can require expensive quantum mechanical calculations. GeoTMI addresses this practical obstacle by training models to work with easier-to-obtain geometries, including those produced by lower-level calculations.

The framework treats these cheaper geometries as corrupted versions of the correct geometry. Starting from the idea that correct geometry best describes the target property, its training objective seeks to maximize mutual information among the correct geometry, corrupted geometry, and property. It also explicitly updates the corrupted positions through successive graph neural network layers so that the input approaches the correct geometry.

This combines property prediction with a structured denoising process, connecting geometric correction to the information needed for the target. The authors evaluate GeoTMI with three-dimensional graph neural networks on molecular properties, a chemical reaction property, and relaxed energy in a heterogeneous catalytic system. They report consistent accuracy improvements across these tasks, supporting the usefulness of learning from more accessible geometric inputs.
neurips-2023-geotmi-predicting-quantum-c.tldr: GeoTMI improves quantum chemical property prediction from accessible geometries by learning to denoise positions while preserving property-relevant information.

paragraphs: Motion perception involves interpreting visual changes in terms of their underlying causes, such as self-motion. This paper investigates whether hierarchical generative models provide a useful account of that process in the primate brain. The authors introduce Retinal Optic Flow Learning, a synthetic-data framework that gives them control over motion statistics and the causes producing them.

They develop a hierarchical variational autoencoder and compare it with alternative models on recovering motion causes and predicting neuronal responses. By changing architectures, training losses, and stimulus causal structure, they examine how these choices affect learned representations. Hierarchical latent structure makes the underlying variables easier to recover through linear decoding, with sparse and more disentangled representations.

The hierarchical model also exceeds previous state-of-the-art models in predicting neuronal responses and shows sparse relationships between latent variables and neurons. These findings depend on the causal structure of the stimuli, so architecture alone does not explain brain-model alignment. The results suggest that hierarchical Bayesian inference is a useful account of motion understanding and that ecologically relevant stimulus statistics are important to that account.
neurips-2023-hierarchical-vaes-provide-a.tldr: Hierarchical VAEs better recover motion causes and predict primate neuronal responses, with benefits depending on the stimuli's causal structure.

paragraphs: A neuron's activity can change substantially while its gene expression remains relatively stable in the adult brain. This motivates separating a neuron's persistent identity from the changing inputs it receives. The paper learns a stable representation for each neuron using both its own activity and the dynamics of the surrounding population.

The method fits dynamical models through self-supervised learning. Its population summary is invariant to neuron ordering and population size, allowing the representation to use collective activity without depending on a fixed arrangement of recorded cells. Implicit representations and self-supervision support robust inference when recording sessions only partly overlap, activity varies across trials, or molecular labels for later supervised tasks are scarce.

The authors evaluate the approach on a public mouse cortical dataset containing activity recordings and transcriptomic labels. Relative to the state of the art, they report improvements exceeding 35% for transcriptomic subclass prediction and 20% for class prediction. These findings support the idea that activity interpreted in its population context contains useful information about relatively stable neuronal identity.
neurips-2023-learning-time-invariant-rep.tldr: Self-supervised modeling of individual and population activity learns stable neuron representations that improve transcriptomic identity prediction.

paragraphs: Generative retrieval answers a search query by generating document identifiers. The way those identifiers are assigned is therefore central to retrieval: the model must decode an identifier that precisely selects the intended document. GenRet learns these identifiers from document meaning instead of relying on a hand-designed tokenization rule.

The method uses discrete autoencoding to represent documents as short sequences of discrete tokens. A progressive training scheme accounts for the sequential generation of identifiers, while diverse clustering techniques stabilize learning. The goal is to embed document semantics in the identifiers so that the retrieval model can connect queries to documents through the meaning represented by their codes.

Experiments cover NQ320K, MS MARCO, and BEIR. GenRet sets a new state of the art on NQ320K, substantially improves retrieval of unseen documents relative to generative retrieval baselines, and outperforms comparable baselines on the other two datasets. These findings support learned semantic identifiers as a way to improve both retrieval accuracy and generalization beyond documents already encountered during training.
neurips-2023-learning-to-tokenize-for-ge.tldr: GenRet learns short, meaning-bearing document identifiers to improve generative retrieval and generalization to unseen documents.

paragraphs: Open-set object recognition asks whether an object belongs to a class encountered during training or to an unfamiliar class. A central difficulty is reliance on spurious discriminative features: features that help separate training classes but can mislead recognition beyond those familiar categories. LMC addresses this problem through collaboration among pretrained large models.

The motivating idea is that models pretrained through different paradigms can hold rich but distinct implicit knowledge. LMC brings several off-the-shelf models together in a training-free framework and includes designs for extracting that knowledge. Its proposed resource is therefore the complementary information already present in existing models, with cross-assessment forming part of the collaboration described in the title.

The authors report extensive experiments supporting the framework's effectiveness. The stated contribution is an approach to open-set recognition that uses differences among pretrained models to address misleading feature reliance without additional framework training. This matters because recognizing unfamiliarity requires more than confidently distinguishing known classes; the evidence used for that judgment must remain useful when the object falls outside those classes.
neurips-2023-lmc-large-model-collaborati.tldr: LMC collaborates across off-the-shelf large models to improve open-set object recognition without additional training.

paragraphs: Feedback graphs describe which losses a learner observes after choosing an action. This paper studies strongly observable undirected graphs and sharpens worst-case regret bounds. The graph's independence number, alpha, captures a structural aspect of feedback availability, connecting the experts case at alpha = 1 to the bandit case at alpha = K, where K is the number of actions.

The new upper bound scales as the square root of alpha times T times (1 + ln(K/alpha)), where T is the learning horizon. It matches known rates at both endpoints and improves how the bound changes between them. The algorithm uses follow-the-regularized-leader with a Tsallis-entropy parameter chosen according to alpha, supported by a new variance bound.

The techniques also handle changing graphs without advance knowledge of their independence numbers. A separate lower-bound argument reduces the problem to multitask learning and establishes a necessary logarithmic factor when alpha is below K. Together, these results clarify which costs come from limited feedback and which logarithmic dependencies cannot simply be removed.
neurips-2023-on-the-minimax-regret-for-o.tldr: Sharper upper and lower regret bounds clarify how online learning difficulty varies between full-information and bandit feedback.

paragraphs: Event prediction can benefit from knowledge about how one type of event affects another. This paper studies how to incorporate qualitative causal relationships into transformers for multivariate event sequences. An example is knowing that the occurrence of one event type increases future occurrences of another, even without specifying a precise numerical effect.

The authors propose a transformer-based causal inference framework for temporal event sequences, provide theoretical justification, and show how to obtain unbiased estimates of their proposed measure. The approach explicitly brings pairwise causal knowledge into the model. This connects information about relationships between event types with the task of predicting how a sequence will develop.

Experiments report higher prediction accuracy than several state-of-the-art models by using this causal-pair information. The paper also explores societal event sequences generated by a large language model, showing how a causal knowledge graph can support prediction in those sequences. These results support the practical value of incorporating qualitative causal structure into event models, including the particular generated-sequence application studied.
neurips-2023-pairwise-causality-guided-t.tldr: The framework incorporates qualitative pairwise causal knowledge into transformers to improve prediction of multivariate event sequences.

paragraphs: LiDAR captures only part of a scene, so point-cloud pretraining must learn from incomplete spatial information. Images can provide richer semantic evidence, but occlusion complicates matching image pixels with three-dimensional points. PRED uses images to assist outdoor point-cloud pretraining while explicitly accounting for this obstacle.

Its core mechanism is semantic rendering conditioned on a bird's-eye-view feature map. Through neural rendering, semantic information from images supervises the point-cloud representation in an occlusion-aware way. This ties the representation to richer scene meaning while addressing the ambiguity created by incomplete LiDAR measurements. The framework also masks 95% of points during pretraining, which the authors report further improves performance.

Experiments on several large-scale datasets show significant improvements over prior point-cloud pretraining methods for three-dimensional perception tasks. The findings support using image semantics as a training resource for point-cloud encoders, with visibility handled as part of the learning problem. That combination is particularly relevant where annotating point clouds is costly and the captured points provide only a partial account of the scene.
neurips-2023-pred-pre-training-via-seman.tldr: PRED improves outdoor point-cloud pretraining through occlusion-aware semantic rendering supervised by images and extensive point masking.

paragraphs: Input-convex neural networks constrain their input-output mapping to be convex. Their construction uses nonnegative weights and nondecreasing convex activation functions, making their training behavior different from that of ordinary networks. Standard initialization strategies implicitly assume centered weights, which makes those strategies poorly suited to these constraints.

The paper derives an initialization specifically for input-convex networks by analyzing signal propagation through layers with nonnegative weights. It extends signal propagation theory beyond the assumption that weights come from a centered distribution. This addresses the network's actual weight structure when choosing its starting parameters, rather than applying a prescription derived under incompatible assumptions.

Experiments show faster learning and better generalization with the proposed initialization. The authors also find that correctly initialized input-convex networks can train without skip connections, challenging the belief that those connections are required. In a drug discovery application, the networks enable more effective exploration of molecular latent space. The findings connect an initialization choice to both improved training behavior and a useful application of the resulting convex models.
neurips-2023-principled-weight-initialis.tldr: An initialization derived for nonnegative weights accelerates input-convex network learning and improves generalization in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Few-shot classification must represent a class using only a small number of examples. Prototype-based methods often do this by averaging example representations, but that estimate can be fragile when examples are scarce. ProtoDiff learns a task-conditioned process for generating class prototypes instead of relying solely on a deterministic average.

During meta-training, the method optimizes prototypes to fit individual tasks closely. These task-specific, overfitted prototypes provide targets for a diffusion process learned in prototype space. The process learns a relationship between ordinary prototypes and these optimized targets. For a new task, it gradually generates prototypes from random noise while conditioning on the available labeled examples.

The authors also introduce residual prototype learning, using sparsity in prototype differences to accelerate training and improve performance. Ablation studies support the method's ability to capture prototype distributions and improve generalization. Reported results establish new state-of-the-art performance in within-domain, cross-domain, and few-task few-shot classification. The findings suggest that learning how class representations should vary across tasks can improve classification when direct prototype estimation has little evidence to work with.
neurips-2023-protodiff-learning-to-learn.tldr: ProtoDiff learns a task-guided diffusion process that generates class prototypes for improved few-shot classification.

paragraphs: Experience replay trains reinforcement learning agents using stored interactions, but the agent must first collect those interactions. Limited experience can make even small networks overfit, particularly early in learning. SynthER addresses this shortage by using a diffusion model to generate additional synthetic experience from the agent's collected data.

The method expands the training data available to replay-based learning. The authors evaluate it in both offline settings, where learning uses an existing dataset, and online settings, where agents continue collecting experience. Their evaluations cover environments with proprioceptive observations as well as environments represented through pixels, testing the approach across different forms of input.

For small offline datasets, synthetic expansion produces large reported improvements and allows larger networks to be trained effectively. Online agents can perform many more learning updates relative to the amount of newly collected data, improving sample efficiency without changes to the underlying learning algorithm. These findings support synthetic replay as a way to make more use of limited real experience and to support greater model capacity in the evaluated settings.
neurips-2023-synthetic-experience-replay.tldr: SynthER uses diffusion-generated experience to improve replay-based reinforcement learning from limited collected data.

paragraphs: Tabular data presents a different modeling problem from text: its fields can contain heterogeneous kinds of information, and some entries may be missing. TabMT adapts masked transformers to generate synthetic tables while addressing both characteristics. The objective is to produce useful artificial data across a broad range of dataset sizes.

The model uses a masked-transformer design with improved masking techniques that enable generation. Handling missing data is built into the design, alongside support for heterogeneous fields. This makes the masking mechanism central to the proposed approach: it supports a model designed around incomplete and varied tabular information while also providing the means to generate synthetic data.

The authors report state-of-the-art performance on datasets ranging from extremely small to extremely large. They also evaluate privacy-focused applications and report high-quality generated data with superior privacy tradeoffs. These are empirical findings about the balance between data quality and privacy in the evaluated settings. Together, they support masked transformers as a useful approach to synthetic tabular generation across differing data scales and application requirements.
neurips-2023-tabmt-generating-tabular-da.tldr: TabMT generates synthetic tables with a masked transformer that handles heterogeneous fields and missing data, with favorable reported quality–privacy tradeoffs.

paragraphs: A model can predict accurately yet provide information that is poorly suited to the decision made from its predictions. TaskMet addresses this mismatch between prediction quality and downstream usefulness. It uses the downstream task loss to learn a metric that shapes the loss used to train the prediction model.

The learned metric changes which information the training process emphasizes. According to the paper, this does not change the optimal prediction model itself; it changes model learning so that information important to the task receives greater attention. Predictions remain in their original prediction space, preserving the model's predictive role while making training sensitive to how its outputs will be used.

The authors validate the approach in decision-focused learning for portfolio optimization and budget allocation, and in reinforcement learning with noisy environments and distracting states. These settings examine the same core issue: predictive details differ in their importance to the eventual task. The contribution is a way to let downstream objectives guide the geometry of prediction loss while retaining the original prediction target.
neurips-2023-taskmet-task-driven-metric-.tldr: TaskMet learns a task-informed prediction-loss metric that emphasizes useful information without changing the optimal prediction model.

paragraphs: Point-cloud segmentation includes assigning semantic categories, separating individual instances, and combining these goals in panoptic segmentation. These tasks have often used separate architectures, making methods less flexible across tasks. ProtoSEG unifies them by treating segmentation as classification at different levels of granularity.

The model uses a Transformer to extract representations for individual points and dynamically learns class prototypes suited to the end task. It optimizes distances between these representations and prototypes, giving the different segmentation problems a shared computational structure. The prototype design also provides a transparent way to relate point assignments to learned class representatives.

Experiments show ProtoSEG outperforming concurrent specialized architectures on three-dimensional point-cloud benchmarks. Semantic segmentation results span S3DIS, ScanNet V2, and SemanticKITTI; instance results cover S3DIS and ScanNet V2; and panoptic results include SemanticKITTI. The reported performance supports the central claim that a common prototype-based formulation can be competitive across all three tasks. Its significance is the combination of a simpler shared design with strong task-specific results, reducing the need to treat each segmentation setting as an entirely separate architecture problem.
neurips-2023-unified-3d-segmenter-as-pro.tldr: ProtoSEG unifies semantic, instance, and panoptic point-cloud segmentation through learned prototypes and point-level classification.

paragraphs: Sparse variational Gaussian processes approximate a full Gaussian process using a smaller set of inducing points. More inducing points can improve approximation fidelity, but they also increase computational costs and optimization difficulty. This paper investigates another way to improve the approximation: making the conditional distributions used for training and prediction more flexible.

The key change separates the parameterization of the predictive mean from that of the predictive covariance. These describe the prediction's central value and its uncertainty structure. Learning independent parameters for them gives the conditional distributions additional freedom. The authors derive evidence lower bounds for these more flexible conditionals, providing objectives for fitting the resulting models.

The paper supplies two concrete applications of the decoupled conditionals and evaluates the approach on regression and Bayesian optimization tasks. The added flexibility improves empirical performance across the reported applications. The contribution is thus a different design choice within sparse Gaussian-process inference: improving how predictions and uncertainty are parameterized, alongside the familiar option of increasing the number of inducing points.
neurips-2023-variational-gaussian-proces.tldr: Decoupling conditional mean and covariance parameters makes sparse variational Gaussian processes more flexible and improves reported predictive performance.
